terms.name: AI / machine learning / deep learning
terms.definition: AI is the broad field; machine learning learns patterns from data; deep learning uses neural networks with many layers.
terms.example: Sorting messages by learned patterns is machine learning. A modern language model is a deep-learning system.
terms.trap: These labels describe overlapping levels of a field, not three competing products.

terms.name: Model vs application
terms.definition: A model performs learned computation. An application adds an interface, files, tools and rules around one or more models.
terms.example: A chat app may search the web using a separate tool, then ask a model to write the answer.
terms.trap: A product feature is not necessarily a capability inside the model weights.

terms.name: LLM — large language model
terms.definition: A language model with many learned parameters that models token sequences and can generate text.
terms.example: The same model can draft a letter, explain a paragraph or translate a sentence.
terms.trap: Fluent output is not a guarantee of correct facts or sound reasoning.

terms.name: Token
terms.definition: A unit processed by a model; text tokens can be words, word fragments, characters or other pieces.
terms.example: A long technical word may use several tokens even though you count it as one word.
terms.trap: There is no universal tokens-per-word ratio across languages and tokenizers.

terms.name: Tokenizer
terms.definition: The system that converts input into the token IDs a model processes.
terms.example: Two models can split the same supplier specification differently.
terms.trap: Token counts can differ even when the visible text is identical.

terms.name: Parameters / weights
terms.definition: Learned numerical settings that shape how a neural network processes inputs. A parameter count describes how many such values it has.
terms.example: An 8B model has roughly eight billion parameters.
terms.trap: More parameters do not automatically mean a better result on your task.

terms.name: Embedding
terms.definition: A numerical representation of an item, such as a token or document, useful for comparing or processing meaning-related patterns.
terms.example: A document search system compares a question’s representation with representations of stored passages.
terms.trap: Similar representations do not prove that two statements are equally true.

terms.name: Attention
terms.definition: A learned mechanism that weights and combines relevant representations.
terms.example: To interpret “it,” useful context may include a noun mentioned earlier in the sentence.
terms.trap: Attention weights are not a complete explanation of a model’s decision.

terms.name: Transformer
terms.definition: A neural-network architecture using attention and other layers to process sequences.
terms.example: Many later language models adapt this architecture for understanding or generating text.
terms.trap: A shared architecture name does not mean all models use the same training data or design.

terms.name: Multimodal
terms.definition: Able to process or generate more than one type of information, such as text, images, audio or video.
terms.example: A model reads a chart image and answers a written question about it.
terms.trap: Supported input types and tool access differ between particular models and products.

terms.name: Pre-training
terms.definition: The broad initial training stage that learns reusable patterns from data.
terms.example: A model develops general language capabilities before being adapted for a narrower role.
terms.trap: Pre-training is not the same as opening your document during a conversation.

terms.name: Fine-tuning
terms.definition: Further training that updates a pre-trained model or trainable additions using selected examples.
terms.example: Train on examples of well-written inspection reports to improve a consistent report style.
terms.trap: It is not a reliable substitute for retrieving a changing inventory database.

terms.name: Post-training
terms.definition: Training stages after broad pre-training, often used to improve instruction following, preferences or task behavior.
terms.example: A model learns to answer requests in a more useful format.
terms.trap: The label covers different methods; it does not identify a single recipe.

terms.name: Inference
terms.definition: Running a trained model to produce outputs from new inputs.
terms.example: You submit a question and receive a generated answer.
terms.trap: Ordinary inference does not necessarily change the model’s weights.

terms.name: Loss
terms.definition: A numerical training objective that measures how poorly a model performs according to a chosen rule.
terms.example: Training adjusts weights to reduce prediction error on examples.
terms.trap: Lower training loss does not guarantee better real-world usefulness.

terms.name: RLHF — reinforcement learning from human feedback
terms.definition: Uses human feedback, often comparisons of outputs, to help train model behavior through reinforcement learning.
terms.example: People prefer one answer to another, helping shape a training signal.
terms.trap: Preferred answers are not always factually correct.

terms.name: Distillation
terms.definition: Training a student model using outputs or signals from a teacher model.
terms.example: A smaller model learns from examples produced by a stronger model.
terms.trap: The student need not preserve all of the teacher’s abilities or limitations in the same way.

terms.name: LoRA / adapters
terms.definition: Parameter-efficient adaptation that trains small additions or low-rank updates while much of the base model remains fixed.
terms.example: Customize a general model without updating every original parameter.
terms.trap: Training fewer parameters does not eliminate the need to run or store the base model.

terms.name: Prompt
terms.definition: The input instructions and context supplied to a model.
terms.example: Ask for a comparison table and provide the quotations to compare.
terms.trap: Better wording cannot supply missing evidence by itself.

terms.name: Context window
terms.definition: The amount of token-based context a model can handle within its supported request limits.
terms.example: A request includes instructions, conversation history and excerpts from a paper.
terms.trap: A large advertised limit does not guarantee perfect retrieval of every detail.

terms.name: RAG — retrieval-augmented generation
terms.definition: Retrieves relevant external material and supplies it to a model when generating an answer.
terms.example: Find passages in an equipment manual before answering a maintenance question.
terms.trap: Bad retrieval or unsupported generation can still produce a wrong answer.

terms.name: Hallucination
terms.definition: Generated content that is incorrect or unsupported, sometimes presented convincingly.
terms.example: A plausible-looking research citation turns out not to exist.
terms.trap: Confidence, detail and good formatting do not establish truth.

terms.name: Reasoning tokens / test-time compute
terms.definition: Extra computation used while answering, sometimes involving additional generated tokens, attempts or tool calls.
terms.example: A difficult problem receives more work before the final answer is returned.
terms.trap: More computation can cost more and still lead to an incorrect answer.

terms.name: Temperature
terms.definition: A sampling setting that changes how sharply a model’s next-token probabilities are favored.
terms.example: Lower settings often produce more repeatable wording; higher settings can increase variation.
terms.trap: It is not a truthfulness control, and not every model exposes it.

terms.name: Agent
terms.definition: A system in which a model helps choose actions and use tools over multiple steps toward a goal.
terms.example: Read files, run a calculation, inspect the result and revise a report.
terms.trap: The term is used loosely; ask which actions and checks the system actually performs.

terms.name: Workflow vs agent
terms.definition: A workflow follows a more predefined sequence; an agent chooses more of its next steps dynamically.
terms.example: A fixed invoice extraction pipeline differs from an assistant investigating why numbers disagree.
terms.trap: An agent is not automatically the best choice for a predictable, simple task.

terms.name: Tool / API
terms.definition: A tool performs an external action or returns information. An API is a defined way for software to request such operations.
terms.example: A spreadsheet tool calculates totals; a search tool retrieves pages.
terms.trap: Writing “I sent the email” is different from a successful email tool action.

terms.name: Harness / orchestration
terms.definition: The surrounding system that supplies tools, manages context and runs the model’s work loop.
terms.example: The same model can perform differently with different search tools and retry rules.
terms.trap: A benchmark result may reflect the whole setup, not just the underlying model.

terms.name: Verification
terms.definition: Checking outputs against evidence, tests, constraints or observed results.
terms.example: Reconcile the extracted quotation total with the original document and a calculation.
terms.trap: A second generated opinion is not independent verification by itself.

terms.name: GPU / accelerator
terms.definition: Hardware designed to execute many numerical operations in parallel, widely used to train and run neural networks.
terms.example: A server uses accelerators for model computation while other software manages files and requests.
terms.trap: Chip count alone does not describe usable performance; memory, networking and software also matter.

terms.name: VRAM / HBM / model memory
terms.definition: VRAM is device memory; HBM is a high-bandwidth memory technology used by many accelerators. Running models needs memory for weights and other state.
terms.example: A model may need space for stored parameters, conversation caches and temporary calculations.
terms.trap: A weights-only size estimate is not a full hardware requirement.

terms.name: Quantization
terms.definition: Represents some numerical values with fewer bits to reduce storage or computation costs.
terms.example: A lower-bit representation can reduce the memory occupied by model weights.
terms.trap: Quality and speed depend on the method and hardware; fewer bits are not a universal speed guarantee.

terms.name: MoE — mixture of experts
terms.definition: A network that selects particular expert subnetworks for each input rather than activating all experts every time.
terms.example: A router sends a token through a small subset of available experts.
terms.trap: Experts are learned subnetworks, not necessarily human-readable subject departments.

terms.name: Total vs active parameters
terms.definition: Total parameters describe stored capacity; active parameters describe the portion used for a particular computation under the model’s definition.
terms.example: A sparse model may store many experts but use only a subset for a token.
terms.trap: The active count is not the amount of memory needed to store the whole model.

terms.name: KV cache
terms.definition: Stored attention information from earlier tokens, reused during later generation steps.
terms.example: An ongoing conversation reuses information rather than recomputing every previous step from scratch.
terms.trap: This working state is not the same thing as permanent personal memory.

terms.name: Prefill vs decode
terms.definition: Prefill processes supplied input; decode generates new output tokens in successive steps.
terms.example: You first wait for an answer to start, then watch it stream.
terms.trap: Long input and long output stress a serving system differently.

terms.name: Latency / TTFT
terms.definition: Latency is waiting time; time to first token measures how long it takes until generation begins.
terms.example: A reply can start quickly yet take a long time to finish.
terms.trap: One waiting-time metric does not describe the entire experience.

terms.name: Throughput / batching
terms.definition: Throughput measures work completed per time; batching processes requests together to improve resource use.
terms.example: A server handles many users concurrently rather than dedicating a whole accelerator to each one.
terms.trap: Higher total throughput does not necessarily mean a shorter wait for each user.

terms.name: Benchmark
terms.definition: A defined set of evaluation tasks and scoring rules.
terms.example: A coding benchmark checks solutions under a particular set of tools, budgets and tests.
terms.trap: One leaderboard score is not a universal measure of intelligence or business value.

terms.name: Ablation
terms.definition: An experiment that changes or removes a component to study its contribution.
terms.example: Compare the same training setup with and without a new attention mechanism.
terms.trap: Several simultaneous changes make it harder to identify which change caused a gain.

terms.name: Checkpoint / model weights
terms.definition: A saved model state that can be loaded for further training or inference.
terms.example: A research team releases a downloadable version of its trained model.
terms.trap: A checkpoint alone may not include training data, full training code or deployment software.

terms.name: Open weights / open source
terms.definition: Open weights make model parameters available under stated terms. Open-source claims require checking what materials and permissions are actually provided.
terms.example: A downloadable model may still have a custom license or restricted uses.
terms.trap: Availability, permission to use commercially, and reproducibility are separate questions.

terms.name: Preprint / technical report / announcement
terms.definition: These formats publish different kinds of information: research findings, technical documentation or product claims.
terms.example: A release blog can establish an announcement date without providing a complete reproducible experiment.
terms.trap: Public availability does not by itself establish peer review or independent replication.

terms.name: FLOPs / compute budget
terms.definition: FLOPs count floating-point operations; a compute budget describes the computational work available or used.
terms.example: Two training runs may allocate a fixed budget differently between model size and training data.
terms.trap: An operation count is not a direct measurement of wall-clock time or money.

terms.name: Gradient
terms.definition: A vector of partial derivatives giving the local sensitivity of a scalar objective to its parameters.
terms.example: For L=(x²+3y²)/2, the gradient is (x,3y). At (1,1), a small change in y has three times the first-order effect of the same change in x.
terms.trap: The gradient uses local information. Curvature determines how far a linear prediction stays accurate.

terms.name: Gradient descent
terms.definition: Update a parameter vector by subtracting a multiple of the gradient of the loss.
terms.example: At (1,1), subtracting 0.1(1,3) gives (0.9,0.7). Inspect the orange path in the loss-surface model.
terms.trap: Large steps can overshoot a minimum even with the correct gradient.

terms.name: Learning rate
terms.definition: The multiplier that converts a gradient into a parameter update.
terms.example: With gradient 4, a learning rate of 0.05 makes a step of magnitude 0.2.
terms.trap: A single learning rate produces different step lengths as gradient magnitudes change.

terms.name: Curvature and Hessian
terms.definition: The Hessian contains second partial derivatives. Its eigenvalues describe directional curvature at a point for a smooth scalar loss.
terms.example: For (x²+3y²)/2 the Hessian is diagonal with entries 1 and 3. The bowl is steeper along y.
terms.trap: For a positive-definite quadratic, constant-step gradient descent converges for 0 < η < 2/λmax. A general neural loss can have different local geometry.

terms.name: Stochastic gradient descent
terms.definition: Estimate the loss gradient using sampled training examples and update the weights using that estimate.
terms.example: Use 32 examples to estimate the direction for one training step.
terms.trap: The sampled direction can differ from the full-data gradient at the same weights.

terms.name: Mini-batch
terms.definition: A group of examples used together to estimate a training update.
terms.example: A batch of eight equally weighted losses contributes their mean to a simple objective.
terms.trap: Gradient accumulation can combine several small batches before one update.

terms.name: Epoch
terms.definition: One pass through the training dataset under a specified sampling scheme.
terms.example: With 1,000 examples and batches of 50, one full pass has 20 batches.
terms.trap: For a data stream, reporting training tokens or steps can be clearer than reporting epochs.

terms.name: Backpropagation
terms.definition: Apply the chain rule backward through a computation to obtain gradients.
terms.example: If u=wx and L=u²/2, then ∂L/∂w=u·x.
terms.trap: The optimizer uses these derivatives to choose an update.

terms.name: Regularization
terms.definition: Discourage some forms of model complexity during fitting to improve generalization.
terms.example: Adding λ‖w‖² to the data loss penalizes large weights.
terms.trap: Excessive regularization can also hurt performance on unseen data.

terms.name: Vector
terms.definition: An ordered collection of components in a coordinate system.
terms.example: The toy point (2,1,0) has three coordinates. A learned embedding may have hundreds or thousands.
terms.trap: Feature scales affect distance comparisons between points.

terms.name: Euclidean norm
terms.definition: The length of a vector, computed as the square root of the sum of its squared coordinates.
terms.example: The vector (3,4) has length 5. Dividing it by 5 gives a unit vector.
terms.trap: Normalizing a zero vector requires special handling.

terms.name: Dot product
terms.definition: Multiply matching components and sum them. The result depends on both direction and length.
terms.example: (1,2)·(3,4)=11. Multiplying one vector by two doubles the dot product.
terms.trap: High vector norms can dominate scores even when directions differ.

terms.name: Cosine similarity
terms.definition: Measure the angle between two nonzero vectors by dividing their dot product by their lengths.
terms.example: (1,0) and (5,0) have cosine similarity 1. Turn one through 90° and the score becomes 0.
terms.trap: Similarity depends on the representation learned for the task.

terms.name: Euclidean distance
terms.definition: Measure straight-line separation as the norm of the difference of two vectors.
terms.example: Between (1,2) and (4,6), the difference is (3,4) and the distance is 5.
terms.trap: On unit vectors, squared distance equals 2−2 cos θ. With varying lengths, rankings can change.

terms.name: Softmax
terms.definition: Convert real-valued scores into positive weights that sum to one using exponentials and normalization.
terms.example: Three equal scores each receive weight 1/3. Adding the same constant to all scores preserves every weight.
terms.trap: A normalized score can still be a poor estimate of real-world probability.

terms.name: Causal mask
terms.definition: Restrict attention at a sequence position to allowed positions, typically itself and earlier tokens.
terms.example: At token four, block scores for positions five and later before normalizing attention weights.
terms.trap: The mask enforces an information boundary even when training positions are processed together.

terms.name: Positional encoding
terms.definition: Give a sequence model information about token order or relative position.
terms.example: The original Transformer adds sinusoidal signals at multiple frequencies to token embeddings.
terms.trap: Later architectures encode position in other ways, so check the paper’s actual mechanism.

terms.name: Train, validation and test splits
terms.definition: Use separate examples to fit weights, select a design and estimate final performance.
terms.example: Tune a retrieval threshold on validation queries, then evaluate once on held-out test queries.
terms.trap: Repeatedly tuning against the test set compromises its independence.

terms.name: Overfitting
terms.definition: Fit patterns specific to training examples that fail to generalize to new cases.
terms.example: Training error keeps falling while validation error begins to climb.
terms.trap: Check distribution shifts and label quality when interpreting a train–validation gap.

terms.name: Precision
terms.definition: Among items predicted positive, the fraction that are truly positive.
terms.example: If 8 of 10 retrieved pages are relevant, retrieval precision is 8/10.
terms.trap: Precision alone omits relevant items the system missed.

terms.name: Recall
terms.definition: Among all truly positive items, the fraction successfully found.
terms.example: If the collection contains 20 relevant pages and retrieval returns 8, recall is 8/20.
terms.trap: Computing recall requires knowing or estimating how many relevant items exist.

terms.name: Baseline
terms.definition: A reference method used to measure what a new design adds.
terms.example: Compare a retrieval assistant with the same generator receiving no retrieved passages.
terms.trap: Match evaluation tasks, budgets and scoring rules for a meaningful comparison.

terms.name: Data leakage
terms.definition: Information unavailable at the intended prediction time enters training or evaluation inputs.
terms.example: A classifier predicting late deliveries accidentally sees the final arrival date.
terms.trap: Leakage can inflate measured performance even when the model code is correct.

terms.name: Calibration
terms.definition: Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed outcome frequencies across comparable cases.
terms.example: Among many predictions assigned about 80% confidence, roughly 80% should be correct for good calibration in that range.
terms.trap: Calibration can change when the deployment population changes.

terms.name: State-space model
terms.definition: A system whose evolving internal state summarizes past inputs and determines its output.
terms.example: For dh/dt = −ah + 1, h(0)=0, the response approaches 1/a with time constant 1/a.
terms.trap: This scalar illustration has fixed coefficients. Selective sequence models can change their dynamics with the input.

facts.title: The AI industry has several layers
facts.fact: Hardware, model development, hosting, tools and applications create different kinds of value. One company may operate at several layers.
facts.example: A faster chip, a new model and a better document workflow solve different problems.
facts.ask: Which layer improved, and does that improvement reach the user’s actual task?

facts.title: A model release is not a complete product
facts.fact: Useful products add retrieval, software integration, context management, permissions and checks.
facts.example: A model may describe a spreadsheet edit; an application needs tools to perform and verify it.
facts.ask: Are we evaluating the model alone or the full system?

facts.title: A bigger parameter count is not a complete ranking
facts.fact: Capability depends on training, data, architecture, tools and task. Sparse models also distinguish total from active parameters.
facts.example: Two models with similar counts may differ on document extraction or long-running work.
facts.ask: What was tested under comparable conditions?

facts.title: Weights are only part of serving memory
facts.fact: A running system also needs cache and temporary state. Quantization can change some of these costs differently.
facts.example: An 8B model at 16 bits uses about 16 GB for raw weights alone in a simple estimate.
facts.ask: Does the memory number include caches, runtime overhead and concurrency?

facts.title: Cheap tokens do not guarantee cheap finished work
facts.fact: Input, output, cached context, tool use and repeated attempts can all affect the cost of a workflow.
facts.example: An agent that retries many times can cost more than a pricier model that finishes promptly.
facts.ask: What is the cost per accepted result, including checks and retries?

facts.title: Speed is more than one number
facts.fact: Time to first token, output speed, total completion time and shared-server throughput describe different things.
facts.example: An answer may start fast but finish slowly; a busy server may process many requests with longer queues.
facts.ask: Which speed measure was reported, for what input/output lengths and load?

facts.title: Read the evaluation setup before comparing scores
facts.fact: Task versions, tools, prompts, effort, budgets and scoring rules affect measured results.
facts.example: Two scores on similarly named benchmarks may come from different task versions or execution environments.
facts.ask: Were the tasks and adaptation conditions standardized?

facts.title: Context size is capacity, not guaranteed recall
facts.fact: A context window states an input-related limit; it does not demonstrate perfect use of all the information inside it.
facts.example: A model can accept a long manual yet overlook an exception buried near the end.
facts.ask: Was performance tested on the kind of long-document question you need?

facts.title: Retrieval and fine-tuning have different jobs
facts.fact: Retrieval supplies external information during use; fine-tuning changes learned behavior through additional training.
facts.example: Retrieve current stock figures; use training examples to improve a consistent report style.
facts.ask: Do you need fresh evidence, a changed behavior, or both?

facts.title: Downloadable does not mean unrestricted or reproducible
facts.fact: Read the specific license and release materials. Weights, source code, data and commercial permissions are distinct.
facts.example: A release may include weights while leaving important training details unavailable.
facts.ask: What exactly is provided, and under what terms?

facts.title: Product performance does not reveal an undisclosed architecture
facts.fact: Observed results alone cannot establish the internal parameter count, data mix or training method of a closed model.
facts.example: A coding improvement could reflect training, tools or serving changes.
facts.ask: Which technical details were actually disclosed?

facts.title: Announcement, experiment and replication are different evidence
facts.fact: A company can document a release and report experiments. Independent reproduction adds another kind of evidence.
facts.example: A demonstration shows that a task happened in that setup; it does not measure a general success rate.
facts.ask: What is the claim, who measured it, and can the conditions be inspected?

facts.title: More autonomy increases the importance of visible checks
facts.fact: An agent’s tools and permissions determine which real actions it can take. A plan or generated statement is not proof of completion.
facts.example: Before accepting a changed report, inspect the actual file and reconcile important figures.
facts.ask: What evidence shows the intended action completed correctly?

facts.title: The limiting resource changes with the workload
facts.fact: Compute, memory capacity, memory bandwidth and communication can each become the bottleneck. Software and workload shape the result.
facts.example: A change that saves attention memory may help long documents more than short replies.
facts.ask: Which resource limits this particular workload?

examples.title: Compare supplier quotations
examples.goal: Produce a comparable table from three PDF offers.
flow: Retrieve the actual quotations.
Extract product, quantity, currency, unit and delivery terms.
Calculate comparable totals with a calculation tool.
Check each important value against its source page.
examples.lesson: The model helps interpret text; retrieval supplies evidence and calculation tools handle arithmetic. A polished comparison can still contain a currency or unit mistake.

examples.title: Ask about an equipment manual
examples.goal: Find the procedure that applies to a specific model and condition.
flow: Identify the manual version and equipment.
Retrieve the relevant instructions and exceptions.
Answer with source pages and state missing information.
Have a responsible person check the applicable procedure.
examples.lesson: A large context window helps supply material, but it does not guarantee that every exception is applied. Source-specific retrieval can make checking easier.

examples.title: Understand a new research paper
examples.goal: Explain the main contribution without reading every equation first.
flow: Read the problem and main result.
Look up unfamiliar terms.
Compare the new component with the baseline.
Check the experiment and limitations before generalizing.
examples.lesson: Ask what changed, what stayed fixed and what was actually measured. A strong result on one benchmark is not proof of improvement everywhere.

examples.title: Build a weekly operations report
examples.goal: Turn logs and tables into a concise, traceable update.
flow: Gather the week’s authorized records.
Separate recorded facts from plans and missing data.
Calculate totals consistently.
Draft the report and reconcile its figures with the inputs.
examples.lesson: A predictable workflow may be enough. The value often comes from reliable integration and checking, not from adding more autonomous agents.

examples.title: Create a consistent technical writing style
examples.goal: Produce reports with stable terminology and structure.
flow: Start with a clear template and examples in the prompt.
Keep frequently changing facts in external records.
Evaluate representative outputs.
Consider fine-tuning only if simpler methods do not meet the need.
examples.lesson: Behavior and current knowledge are separate requirements. Training is not automatically necessary to get consistent formatting.

quiz.question: You need answers from a frequently changing inventory table. What should supply the current figures?
options: Retrieve or query the current table.
Assume fine-tuning permanently keeps the figures current.
Choose the model with the largest parameter count.
quiz.explanation: Current evidence should come from the current records. Fine-tuning changes a model, but does not automatically synchronize a database.

quiz.question: A sparse model reports 100B total parameters and 10B active per token. Which statement follows?
options: Only 10B parameters need to be stored in every deployment.
Some computation uses a subset; the total storage requirement is a separate question.
It must be ten times faster than a 100B dense model.
quiz.explanation: Active computation and stored capacity are different. Hardware, communication and other work also affect speed.

quiz.question: An app says “I updated the file.” What is the strongest check?
options: Another model agrees that an update sounds plausible.
Inspect the saved file and validate the requested changes.
quiz.explanation: Completion needs evidence from the actual artifact or action, rather than only a statement about it.

quiz.question: Model A scores higher than B on a chart. What should you check first?
options: Whether tasks, versions, tools and budgets are comparable.
Whether A has the more impressive name.
Whether the chart uses a larger font for A.
quiz.explanation: Evaluation conditions affect the meaning of a score. Compare the setup as well as the number.

quiz.question: An 8B model at 16 bits has a raw-weights estimate of roughly 16 GB. What does that number leave out?
options: Nothing; it is a complete deployment requirement.
Caches, temporary state and other serving overhead.
quiz.explanation: The calculator estimates raw weight storage only. Actual serving memory also depends on workload and implementation.

quiz.question: A model accepts a very long document. What can you conclude?
options: Every detail will be recalled and applied correctly.
The model must have trained on that exact document.
The input fits the supported limit; task accuracy still needs checking.
quiz.explanation: Context capacity is useful, but the model can still miss details or make unsupported connections.
